SK2120 A bitwise operator combines members of a consecutively numbered enum

A |, &, ^ or ~ is applied to an enum whose members carry no explicit values, so they are numbered 0, 1, 2, ... and no bit of the result means anything.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since2.0

Why

An enum written enum Color { Red, Green, Blue } numbers its members consecutively, so Red | Green is 0 | 1, which is Green, and Green | Blue is 1 | 2, which is 3 and no declared member at all. The value then fails every switch, every Equals and every ToString, and it does so silently: the operation is legal C#, the compiler says nothing, and the wrong value is only noticed downstream where nothing points back here. ⚠ This is the use site, not the declaration. CA1027 asks a declaration whose values already look like a bit set to carry [Flags], and CA2217 asks a [Flags] declaration to stop declaring values that are not powers of two. Neither can be reached from an enum that was never given explicit values, so neither says a word about the code that combines one — which is the only place the mistake is visible.

Example

Instead of:

enum Color { Red, Green, Blue }

var combined = Color.Green | Color.Blue; // 3, which is not a Color

Write:

[Flags]
enum Color { None = 0, Red = 1, Green = 2, Blue = 4 }

var combined = Color.Green | Color.Blue; // Green | Blue

When it does not fire

⚠ Every member of the enum must be implicitly numbered. One explicit value anywhere in the declaration — Red = 1 — declines the whole enum, because an author who wrote a value down may have been laying out a bit set and the declaration alone cannot say. That exclusion is also what makes this rule provably disjoint from CA1027: CA1027 needs at least three distinct non-zero values that are all powers of two, and consecutive numbering reaches three non-zero values only at 1, 2, 3, where 3 is not a power of two — so CA1027 can never fire on a declaration this rule accepts, and the two can never report one mistake twice. Measured against the SDK at AnalysisMode=All rather than assumed. [Flags] enums are excluded. The operand type is read after unwrapping Nullable<T>; an operand already cast to its underlying integral type is not an enum operation and is not reported. ==, != and the boolean operators are not bitwise combinations of members and are outside the rule. There is no fix: adding [Flags] is a public API change and is usually the wrong answer here, because a consecutively numbered enum is normally a closed choice that should not be combined at all.
